Limb ischemia (hindlimb)

Rodent hindlimb-ischemia experiments reported higher perfusion, capillary density, collateral formation, or tissue repair after PBM, including in diabetic models. Some studies combined PBM with cell therapy, and no human study shows improved walking, wound healing, or limb salvage.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Rodent hindlimb-ischemia experiments reported higher perfusion, capillary density, collateral formation, or tissue repair after PBM, including in diabetic models. Some studies combined PBM with cell therapy, and no human study shows improved walking, wound healing, or limb salvage.

Summary of the Evidence

A focused recheck identified eight PBM publications in a narrow mapping for limb or hindlimb ischemia: five are filed under Angiogenesis, two under Hindlimb ischemia, and one under Hind limb ischemia. All eight include an animal ischemia experiment: seven use mice and one uses rats, while one report also includes a rabbit model. Several papers add cell, ex-vivo, or chick-embryo assays, which overlap with the animal publication count. The records include a related Korean research line using light-treated adipose-derived stem-cell spheroids; these are separate reports but similar interventions and models, so they should not be treated as eight independent research programs. No human clinical PBM study was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

No patient trial has tested PBM for limb ischemia in this mapped set. In particular, there is no direct evidence here that it improves walking, heals ischemic ulcers, avoids amputation, or adds benefit to revascularization and medical care. Results from diabetic-foot-ulcer or wound-healing categories are related but do not count as direct limb-ischemia trials.

Animal evidence

Several mouse experiments report improved blood flow, capillary density, collateral formation, or tissue repair after femoral-artery ligation. A study in diabetic mice used 660 nm light at 1.91 J/cm² for ten minutes on five consecutive days. Treated animals had more than twice the capillary density and measured perfusion of untreated ischemic or diabetic controls, with higher CD31 and VEGF-A markers (Huang et al. 2021).

A 2024 rat experiment used femoral-artery ligation and combined 660 nm red and 808 nm near-infrared light. Several tissue, movement, and temperature measures in PBM-treated ischemic limbs were comparable with non-ischemic controls, but this remains one surgical animal model (Perez et al. 2024).

A 2025 mouse study combined hindlimb ischemia with aortic-ring and chick-embryo assays. Daily 652 nm red-light treatment improved blood-flow recovery at 14 days, while effects at day 5 were minimal (Joniová et al. 2025).

Other reports irradiated adipose-derived stem cells or spheroids before transplantation. They describe greater cell survival, growth-factor secretion, vascular density, or tissue regeneration, but PBM is part of a combined cell-plus-light intervention. Two related Korean spheroid papers have similar models and should be interpreted as a connected research line rather than independent clinical replication (Park et al. 2014 Park et al. 2017).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Some mapped papers include irradiated cell preparations, endothelial-cell assays, an ex-vivo aortic-ring sprouting assay, or a chick-embryo membrane model.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The mapped studies use visible red light at about 652–660 nm and near-infrared light at 808 nm. Red light is visible; 808 nm is invisible near-infrared. Reported doses include 1.91 J/cm² for the five-day diabetic-mouse protocol and 4 J delivered with 660/808 nm light in the rat experiment. The 2025 study used daily 652 nm exposure, but the records do not establish one optimal schedule. Several reports irradiated stem cells before transplantation, a different delivery strategy from shining light through intact human skin. There is no clinical head-to-head or dose-finding evidence, and animal perfusion measurements cannot be assumed to predict walking ability or limb salvage in people.

Interpretation

Several rodent experiments reported higher perfusion, capillary density, collateral-vessel measures, or better tissue repair after induced hindlimb ischemia. In a 2025 mouse study, blood-flow recovery was greater by day 14, while early changes at day 5 were small. Some experiments combined light with cell therapy, so the contribution of PBM alone is uncertain. These are favorable model-level results, not evidence of improved limb outcomes in patients.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow-to-moderate for short-term perfusion recovery in animal models Very low for limb salvage or function in people
Publications and records8 mapped publications

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Several hindlimb-ischemia experiments reported improved perfusion, capillary density, collateral formation, or tissue repair, including in diabetic mice. Effects differed by time point, and some studies combined PBM with cell therapy. This is a positive preclinical pattern, not patient evidence. Replication of light-only protocols and trials measuring wound healing, walking, or limb salvage would strengthen clinical conclusions.
